race.name: Hellhole Gravel Grind Stage Race
race.tagline: Two timed 75-mile forest stages, an optional night prologue, and almost no free speed in coastal South Carolina.

terrain_types: Grassy doubletrack and Palmetto Trail sectors
vitals.start_time: Optional Friday prologue 6:30 PM; Saturday and Sunday stages 9:00 AM
vitals.registration: Online through the organizer's official registration link
vitals.prize_purse: Awards for the top three finishers in each stage-race category
vitals.aid_stations: One stocked aid station on each day's course; limited support
vitals.cutoff_time: Seven hours per stage; five hours for the one-day 45-mile fondo

climate.primary: Warm, humid coastal South Carolina fall
climate.description: October can still bring heat and humidity, and two long remote days amplify hydration and recovery mistakes.

terrain.primary: Fast, flat forest gravel with rough interruptions
terrain.surface: Approximately 90% unpaved forest roads and trails: mostly hard-packed gravel, plus grassy doubletrack, potholes, and Roubaix-rated Palmetto Trail sectors.
features: One aid station per stage and limited cellular service

gravel_god_rating.score_note: The two-day format, remote forest setting, and long history are meaningful. A regional field, limited support, and late route release keep it in Tier 3.

biased_opinion.summary: Hellhole Gravel Grind is a two-day, approximately 150-mile stage race in Francis Marion National Forest, preceded by an optional six-mile night prologue. The terrain is flat but remote, mostly unpaved, lightly supported, and punishing when heat, potholes, or recovery mistakes compound.
strengths: Remote Francis Marion National Forest setting
weaknesses: Routes released only about two weeks before the event
One aid station per day and limited support
biased_opinion.bottom_line: A legitimate regional stage race whose challenge comes from back-to-back 75-mile days, remote navigation, heat, and the recovery clock rather than climbing.

final_verdict.one_liner: Two timed 75-mile forest stages, an optional night prologue, and almost no free speed in coastal South Carolina.
final_verdict.should_you_race: Race it if you want an established, low-elevation stage race where pacing, navigation, fueling, and overnight recovery decide the result.
final_verdict.alternatives: Swamp Fox Gravel Fondo for a single-day Francis Marion event, or a larger destination stage race for deeper fields and more support.

logistics.lodging_strategy: Jamestown has limited lodging. Nearby towns have options.
logistics.food: Small town with limited dining. Stock nutrition.

history.origin_story: Mount Pleasant Velo developed the event from gravel exploration in Francis Marion National Forest and describes it as the first and longest-running gravel stage race in the United States.
history.reputation: An established regional stage race known for a fast prologue, remote forest roads, sparse support, and cumulative two-day attrition.

course_description.character: An optional six-mile night prologue precedes two approximately 75-mile timed stages on mostly unpaved forest roads and trails. The course is flat, remote, unmarked, and released close to race day.

suffering_zones.label: Friday Night Prologue
suffering_zones.desc: A short optional time-bonus effort under lights; open hard without turning six miles into Saturday's fatigue.
suffering_zones.terrain_detail: Six-mile all-gravel out-and-back from the Hellhole Road primitive camp

suffering_zones.label: Saturday Stage Finish
suffering_zones.desc: Begin the overnight recovery clock immediately: carbohydrate, protein, fluid, sodium, clean kit, bike inspection, and sleep.
suffering_zones.terrain_detail: Approximately 75 miles, about 90% unpaved, with one stocked aid station

suffering_zones.label: Sunday Stage Finish
suffering_zones.desc: Race the second 75-mile day only after protecting navigation, hydration, equipment, and attention through the remote final sectors.
suffering_zones.terrain_detail: Approximately 75 miles with a seven-hour cutoff

course_description.signature_challenge: Starting Sunday's second 75-mile stage with enough recovery, hydration, equipment, and restraint left to race rather than unravel.

guide_variables.race_elevation: Not published; the organizer describes the course as pancake flat
guide_variables.race_location: Francis Marion National Forest near Jamestown, South Carolina
guide_variables.race_terrain: Mostly hard-packed gravel with potholes, grassy doubletrack, and Palmetto Trail sectors
guide_variables.race_weather: Warm, humid coastal fall weather with limited shelter and support

non_negotiables.why: Two approximately 75-mile stages require durable pacing and the ability to ride usefully again the next morning.
SC spring/fall means heat and humidity over multiple days.
The optional prologue and first-stage speed cannot be allowed to consume Sunday's race.

topics.heat: Racing in SC heat and humidity

marketplace_variables.race_hook: Two timed 75-mile forest stages, plus an optional night prologue.
marketplace_variables.race_hook_detail: Remote, mostly unpaved Francis Marion roads make recovery, hydration, navigation, and bike care part of the race.

logistics.explanation: Number pickup at 7:00 AM race day creates timeline pressure, especially with mandatory 8:45 AM rider meeting. Jake Andrews dominated the prologue but DNF'd Stage 2 when "his rear derailleur had other plans... the landscape of potholes, gravel and mud can take their toll on riders, bikes, and in this case, jockey pulleys." GPS files provided two weeks prior, but "routes will not be marked" in Francis Marion National Forest where "there are no services (including most cellular)."

length.explanation: Two approximately 75-mile stages create nearly 150 miles of weekend racing, with an optional six-mile Friday prologue for stage racers. The distance is substantial because the second 75-mile start arrives after only one overnight recovery window.

technicality.explanation: "Francis Marion's forest service roads are largely hard packed gravel and pot holes are numerous" with "car sized, bike swallowing potholes" creating constant navigation challenges. Dr. Pain described "dodge left, dodge right, bunny hop, CLANG, DAMN" through the terrain. Singletrack sections include "hiking trail, full of holes, roots and other MTB stuff" along Palmetto Trail, but coastal South Carolina doesn't deliver sustained technical punishment that destroys equipment at scale. Less technical than The Mid South.

elevation.explanation: The organizer describes the course as pancake flat and does not publish a current total climbing figure. Elevation is not the limiter; wind, roughness, heat, and cumulative time on the bike are.

climate.explanation: Sunday Stage 2 in 2015 hit "near 90°F temperatures" that created dangerous conditions - Pfaff Daddy "was getting seriously dehydrated" and "just sat down in the gravel" at the aid station despite being an experienced endurance rider. The 50% DNF rate reflects how heat and humidity compound the physical toll. October timing in coastal South Carolina still delivers punishing conditions that northern riders underestimate. More weather exposure than Belgian Waffle Ride San Diego.

altitude.explanation: Sea-level coastal terrain around Jamestown means altitude plays no role in your suffering equation. Francis Marion National Forest sits in lowland country where the prologue starts at Hellhole Road Primitive Camp near sea level. Race director confirms "despite being pancake flat" the area offers no elevation challenge beyond gentle rolling terrain. Lower altitude than Gravel Worlds — no thin-air concerns.

adventure.explanation: Francis Marion National Forest provides true backcountry isolation where "megafauna such as bear, snakes, boar (and chupacabra)" roam and "there are no services (including most cellular)." Friday night prologue requires lights, navigation by GPS only with unmarked routes, and 90% unpaved roads through New War battlegrounds where "the Swamp Fox made life hell for British troops." Race organizer notes "to say this area is remote is an understatement."

prestige.explanation: Race directors claim this is "the first and longest running gravel stage race in the United States" and "quickly becoming a marquee gravel event," but the field remains small and regional. Former pro Adam Everest from New Zealand won Men 40+ category, providing some competitive depth. The 50% DNF rate and brutal conditions create accomplishment factor, but limited media coverage and small fields keep prestige regional rather than national.

race_quality.explanation: Organization shows structure with proper stage race timing and custom winner jerseys, but execution has gaps. "Stage One started in a panic... the peloton blew past the first turn and was forced to backtrack and chase," and this happened again on Stage Two with "the lead group missing an early turn." Limited aid stations and 7-hour cutoffs for each stage suggest accommodating survival more than competitive racing standards.

experience.explanation: The optional Friday night prologue, two long forest stages, Saturday gathering, and Sunday finish create a complete stage-race weekend rather than a single start-and-finish event.

community.explanation: Mt. Pleasant Velo has organized this since 2013, when "we launched the page within hours, it had over hundred likes." Race directors Chris Moore and Jeff started by exploring Francis Marion on cross bikes: "In retrospect, that was just brutal what it does to your body on a cross bike for that distance." The first year podium "had all three... a road bike, a cross bike, and a mountain bike" plus someone who "did 75 miles on that 36 inch diameter unicycle."

field_depth.explanation: Small fields with limited competitive depth beyond former pro Adam Everest and elite-level riders like Jake Andrews. The lead group had "five people within two minutes of the win" creating tight competition, but overall participation remains modest. "Over half of the field laid down times averaging better than 21 mph" in the prologue suggests some speed, but 7-hour stage cutoffs and 50% DNF rate indicate the event accommodates survival more than deep competitive racing. Less competitive depth than Almanzo 100.

value.explanation: Two long timed stages, the optional night prologue, stage-race timing, post-race food, and a distinctive remote setting provide more event value than a standard one-day regional gravel race.

expenses.explanation: Jamestown has limited lodging, but Charleston access is manageable and the event does not require a shuttle. Riders should budget for two nights, remote-course supplies, lights for the optional prologue, and enough spares to reset the bike between stages.
